summary: Describes an experiment with two new IPv6 Routing headers, collectively the Compact Routing Header: CRH-16 and CRH-32. It aims to show that CRH can be implemented and deployed in production and that its security considerations can be addressed. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Normal routing directions use long addresses. This tries shorter codes for each stop to see if that works in practice.

questions: how does compact routing header work
what is the difference between crh-16 and crh-32
subtitle: Compact encoding for IPv6 source routing with minimal header overhead.

tldr.problem: IPv6 source routing headers that specify packet paths can become large, consuming valuable packet space and increasing header copying costs in routing hardware.
tldr.mechanism: CRH defines two new IPv6 Routing header types (CRH-16 and CRH-32) that encode segment identifiers in 16 or 32 bits, allowing routers to use a Forwarding Information Base to map each SID to an IPv6 address and forwarding method.
tldr.outcome: This is an experimental specification designed to demonstrate that compact routing headers can be implemented and secured in production networks, with results expected within one year of publication.

today: RFC 9631 is an Experimental specification published in August 2024. It is not an Internet Standard and remains subject to evaluation based on implementation and deployment results.

sections.title: IPv6 Routing and Header Overhead
sections.content:
IPv6 Routing headers let the source node specify the path a packet takes to its destination, rather than letting each router independently decide. However, these headers can grow large, particularly when a source needs to specify many waypoints.

Hardware forwarding engines must copy headers from buffer memory to on-chip memory, so larger headers increase the cost of processing each packet. Additionally, because path MTU discovery is not entirely reliable, many IPv6 hosts avoid sending packets larger than 1280 bytes. When packet sizes are limited, large routing headers create excessive overhead.

RFC 9631 proposes the Compact Routing Header (CRH) experiment to show that routers can use much shorter segment identifiers instead of full IPv6 addresses.
sections.eli5: When you write directions for a trip, you can use short codes instead of writing out full addresses. This saves space and lets you fit more waypoints in the same envelope.

sections.title: CRH Header Format and SIDs
sections.content:
The CRH defines two header types: CRH-16 and CRH-32. Both contain standard IPv6 Routing header fields (Next Header, Header Extension Length, Routing Type, and Segments Left), followed by a list of CRH Segment Identifiers (SIDs).

In CRH-16, each SID is encoded in 16 bits. In CRH-32, each SID is encoded in 32 bits. Each SID is an index into a CRH Forwarding Information Base (CRH-FIB) that maps the SID to an IPv6 address and a forwarding method. The SIDs are listed in reverse order: the first SID in the header represents the final interface in the path. Because of this, the Segments Left field can be used directly as an index into the SID list.

The CRH must end on a 64-bit boundary, so the type-specific data field is padded with zeros if necessary.
sections.eli5: The header contains a short list of numbered stops. Each stop number looks up an address and how to get there in a table on the router.

sections.title: The CRH Forwarding Information Base
sections.content:
Each entry in the CRH-FIB contains three components: an IPv6 address, a topological function, and optional parameters for the function.

The IPv6 address can be a Global Unicast Address, Link-Local Unicast address, or Unique Local Address. When the entry is the final address in the path, it can also be a multicast address.

The topological function controls how the router forwards the packet toward that address. For example, a function might specify loose source routing (forward through the least-cost path to that address) or strict source routing (forward through a specific interface to reach that address). Some topological functions require parameters, such as an interface identifier.

The CRH-FIB can be populated by a network operator using the command-line interface, by a central controller using PCEP or NETCONF, or by a distributed routing protocol such as IS-IS, OSPF, or BGP.
sections.eli5: The table tells each router: 'When you see stop number 5, find address 2001:db8::1 and send the packet there using the fast route.'

sections.title: Packet Processing
sections.content:
When a router receives a packet with a CRH, it follows a set of processing rules. First, it checks that the header length is within what the implementation can process. Then it computes the minimum CRH length required based on the Routing Type and Segments Left value.

The router decrements Segments Left, then searches the CRH-FIB for the SID at that index. If the SID is found, the router copies the corresponding IPv6 address into the packet's Destination Address field and submits the packet to the IPv6 forwarding module with the topological function and its parameters.

If the SID is not found in the CRH-FIB, or if any other validation fails, the router discards the packet and sends an ICMPv6 Parameter Problem message to the source address. This prevents misconfigurations or attacks from causing silent packet loss.
sections.eli5: The router reads the next stop number, looks it up, and sends the packet to that address using the method that entry specifies.

sections.title: Security and Trusted Nodes
sections.content:
The CRH specification assumes that a node trusts another node only if both are operated by the same party. Operators typically number their nodes with a small set of IP address prefixes, so nodes identify trusted peers by examining the source address of incoming packets.

Since processing a Routing header from an untrusted source can expose vulnerabilities, nodes MUST deploy Access Control Lists (ACLs) that discard packets containing a CRH when the source address does not identify an interface on a trusted node and the destination address is the local node.

To further protect against spoofed source addresses, nodes MAY also discard CRH packets from trusted sources if they fail an Enhanced Feasible-Path Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding check. However, a network operator deploying CRH MUST implement ACLs on each edge node to discard packets whose source address identifies an interface on a trusted node but the destination is local.

The CRH is compatible with IPv6 Authentication Header processing, because the source node calculates the Integrity Check Value before the packet leaves.
sections.eli5: Only routers you trust can send these packets. Each router checks that the sender is legitimate before following the path directions.

sections.title: Experimental Status and Future Work
sections.content:
RFC 9631 defines an Experimental Protocol. Its purpose is to demonstrate that the CRH can be implemented and deployed in a production network, and to show that security considerations can be addressed with ACLs.

Parties participating in this experiment are asked to publish results within one year of publication, covering deployment effort (whether incremental or network-wide), security effort, performance impact, ACL effectiveness and cost, the CRH-FIB population mechanism, deployment scale, interoperability with other implementations, and the effectiveness of operational tools like PING and Traceroute.

The specification notes that PING and Traceroute operate correctly with CRH, and that TCPDUMP and Wireshark have been extended to support it. Experimental implementations SHOULD use the textual representations defined in the RFC for 16-bit and 32-bit SIDs (such as hexadecimal notation or dotted-decimal notation).
sections.eli5: This is a test to see if short routing codes can work in real networks. Operators will try it and report back within a year on what they learned.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Type of the next header in the packet.

fields.name: Hdr Ext Len
fields.desc: Length of the extension header in 8-octet units (not including the first 8 octets).

fields.name: Routing Type
fields.desc: CRH-16 value is 5; CRH-32 value is 6.

fields.name: Segments Left
fields.desc: Number of segments left in the route; used as index into the SID list.

fields.name: SID[0]
fields.desc: First segment identifier (16 bits in CRH-16).

fields.name: SID[1]
fields.desc: Second segment identifier (16 bits in CRH-16).
